extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (MPEP §2106), including identification and treatment of abstract ideas (mental processes), laws/natural phenomena, products of nature, and the markedly different characteristics analysis. Provides procedures for tentative abstract ideas and required approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental process as an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed map/listing or other steps that can be performed mentally (e.g., with pen and paper) may qualify as a 'mental process' abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should look to the specification to determine whether claimed steps are performable mentally (cases: CyberSource, Flook, University of Florida Research Foundation v. GE, Symantec). If the specification describes the claimed analysis/manipulation of data as being performed mentally or with pen and paper, the step may be an abstract mental process. Example anti-pattern: claiming high-level data-parsing or screening steps that humans could perform without a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim requiring a computer may still recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites performance on a computer can nevertheless recite a mental process (abstract idea) if the underlying concept is one that humans can perform mentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating such claims, examiners should consider the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification to determine whether the invention is described as a concept performed in the human mind and applicant merely claims it: (1) on a generic computer, (2) in a computer environment, or (3) using a computer as a tool. If so, the claim is considered to recite a mental process. Case law: Benson, Mortgage Grader, Voter Verified, Versata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing a mental process on a generic computer
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed steps are human cognitive actions performed on generic computer hardware, the claim may be directed to an abstract idea (mental process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Voter Verified — voting, verifying, and submitting votes were human cognitive actions even though performed on a computer. Versata — pricing determination implemented on general purpose hardware was still 'directed to' the abstract idea. Examine specification for indications that the steps are merely conventional computer implementation of human thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing a mental process in a computer environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that mirror how humans perform a task in an electronic/computer environment may be abstract if, except for generic computer-implemented steps, nothing forecloses human performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Symantec — an electronic post office that screened and redistributed email was analogous to human sorting and thus recited a mental process. FairWarning — rules for detecting improper access mirrored questions humans ask in analogous fraud-detection situations. Look to specification to determine analogy to human actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely use a computer to perform what is otherwise a human-conducted mental process are directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mortgage Grader — anonymous loan shopping concept could be performed by humans without a computer. Berkheimer — parsing and comparing data recited at a high level of generality and merely used computers as a tool. High-level, generalized recitations of data manipulation that do not improve computer functionality indicate use-as-tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both product and process claims may recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Product claims (e.g., systems, computer-readable media) and process claims can both be directed to mental process-type abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Content Extraction (API for extracting/processing hard copy info), Mortgage Grader (system and method), CyberSource (computer-readable medium), Symantec (post office), Voter Verified (self-verifying voting system), Versata (storage media with pricing method). Examiners should understand 'mental processes' as a type of abstract idea, not tied to statutory claim category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative abstract ideas procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: When a limitation appears abstract but does not fall within the enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts, methods of organizing human activity, mental processes), it may be treated as a 'tentative abstract idea.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the claim under the subject matter eligibility framework: - If the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application → not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) → eligible at Pathway B. - If not integrated → directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) → requires Step 2B analysis: if the claim provides an inventive concept (Step 2B: YES) → eligible at Pathway C. - If no inventive concept (Step 2B: NO) → bring application to TC director; a Step 2B rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea must be approved by the TC director (approval indicated in file and Office action uses form paragraph 7.05.017 and TC Director’s signature). The TC Director will notify Patents Management for public notice (e.g., USPTO website). Interviews with the examiner may help; TC Director interview is not required for examiner to withdraw or maintain a rejection; examiner need not obtain approval to withdraw/maintain such a §101 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature; these are judicial exceptions to patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts describe them as 'physical phenomena', 'scientific principles', 'natural laws', and 'products of nature.' Examples provided by case law include isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned animals (Roslin), correlations between genetic variations and alleles, metabolic correlations (Mayo), myeloperoxidase correlation (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health), existence of cffDNA (Ariosa), CYP2D6 genotype correlation (Vanda), electromagnetism to transmit signals (Morse), qualities of bacteria (Funk Bros.). The basic tools of scientific/technological work are not patentable. Not every claim describing a natural ability or quality is an exception — process claims applying or integrating the natural ability (e.g., fractionating/recovering/cryopreserving hepatocytes) may be eligible. Even if a claim recites a law of nature/natural phenomenon, it may still be eligible under Pathways A–C (example: Vanda). If a claim recites a law of nature/natural phenomenon, further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two is required to determine whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature (nature-based products)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature/natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, it may be a 'product of nature' exception; products include naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from natural counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: isolated DNA (Myriad), primers (Ambry Genetics), bacterial mixtures (Funk Bros.), cloned animals (Roslin). Synthetically replicated sequences that are structurally identical to natural ones can still be products of nature. Use the markedly different characteristics analysis (MPEP §2106.04(c)) to evaluate nature-based product limitations. Under BRI, a nature-based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible products; examiners should identify the BRI and, where appropriate, recommend narrowing amendments. For nature-based products that clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception, consider the streamlined analysis of MPEP §2106.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: The markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of Step 2A Prong One: compare the claimed nature-based product to its naturally occurring counterpart to determine whether it possesses 'markedly different characteristics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed nature-based product has markedly different characteristics → claim does not recite a product of nature exception and is eligible at Pathway B (Step 2A: NO), unless the claim recites another judicial exception. For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product, finding a markedly different characteristic obviates further analysis (no Step 2B needed). If the nature-based product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics → the claim recites a product of nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application. When to perform the analysis: apply only to nature-based product limitations (either standalone product claims or product limitations within broader claims); do not overextend the analysis to claims that are not nature-based when viewed as a whole. If the limitation is naturally occurring by definition, the markedly different characteristics analysis is unnecessary because it is directed to a naturally occurring product. Examiners should consider whether the claim recites another exception and whether streamlined eligibility analysis (MPEP §2106.06) is appropriate.
